paper_metadata.title: The prognostic value of resting-state EEG in acute post-traumatic unresponsive states

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the recruitment source, period, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. However, the final sample size is very small (n=18), and while the screening process is documented, the high exclusion rate (only 21 of 139 screened were consented/eligible) suggests a highly selected sample that may not fully represent the broader TBI population.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: We screened all 139 TBI admissions to the intensive care unit of the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, UK, between April 2018 and October 2019.
items.reasoning: The source (ICU admissions at a specific hospital) and the nature of the population (TBI) are clearly stated.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: We screened all 139 TBI admissions... Inclusion criteria of this study required patients to have a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) motor score below 6 (i.e. not obeying commands)
items.reasoning: The recruitment process from the total pool of admissions is transparently reported.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between April 2018 and October 2019.
items.reasoning: The dates are explicitly provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: intensive care unit of the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, UK
items.reasoning: The specific hospital and unit are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria of this study required patients to have a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) motor score below 6... Exclusion criteria were: patients moribund, those with prior history of moderate or severe TBI or neurological disorder...
items.reasoning: Detailed clinical and demographic criteria are listed, including the 'zero time' for EEG (48h to 7 days after sedation hold).

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Of the 139 screened patients, 28 patients were consented onto the study and 21 patients met all inclusion/ exclusion criteria at the time of EEG
items.reasoning: While the flow is described, the small percentage of the total screened population that was actually enrolled (approx 15%) raises concerns about the representativeness of the sample.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 Demographics and clinical data of the patient cohort
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides individual-level data on age, gender, CT grade, GCS, and time since injury.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study had very low attrition. Only one patient was lost to follow-up between the 3-month and 6-month marks, and the reasons for initial exclusion from analysis (technical issues) were reported.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 18 patients were available for follow-up at 3 months... and 17 patients were available for follow-up at 6 months
items.reasoning: 18 out of 19 eligible patients (95%) provided primary outcome data at 3 months.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not describe specific attempts to re-contact the single patient lost at 6 months, though the loss is minimal.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: After excluding data from one patient due to technical issues with the recording... 15 | Male | 59 | 3 | 9 | 6 | 3 | Lost to follow-up
items.reasoning: Technical exclusion is explained; however, the specific reason for the 6-month loss of patient 15 is not detailed beyond the label 'Lost to follow-up'.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.reasoning: Baseline data for the patient lost to follow-up is fully available in Table 1.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: 17 patients were available for follow-up at 6 months
items.reasoning: With only one patient lost, systematic differences between completers and non-completers are unlikely to bias the results significantly.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (EEG metrics) were measured using a standardized, semi-automated pipeline (MOHAWK toolbox). The study included a specific validation step to ensure that low-density EEG (used in patients) reliably reflected high-density EEG (the gold standard in research).

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Relative alpha power (mean over channels), alpha connectivity (median debiased weighted phase lag index over channels)...
items.reasoning: All EEG features are mathematically defined and the frequency bands are specified.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: we first validated a set of measures of oscillatory network features between high-density and low-density resting-state EEG in healthy individuals
items.reasoning: The authors performed a specific validation study to ensure the reliability of the low-density montage used in the clinical setting.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Relative alpha power (mean over channels)...
items.reasoning: The study uses continuous spectral and graph metrics rather than arbitrary thresholds.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A clinical electrophysiologist recorded the EEG data... with a 19-electrode clinically certified EEG system
items.reasoning: Standardized equipment and montage (10/20) were used for all patients.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: After excluding data from one patient due to technical issues with the recording, 18 patients were available
items.reasoning: Only one patient was excluded due to data quality, leaving 18/19 (94.7%) with complete PF data.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation was performed as the dataset for the 18 patients was complete for the analyzed features.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (GOSE) is a standard, validated tool in TBI research. While the assessment was done via telephone (which is standard for GOSE), the study used structured interviews to ensure reliability.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: outcome at 3 and 6 months post-injury... as measured by the Extended Glasgow Outcome Score (GOSE)
items.reasoning: The outcome measure and time points are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: we quantified outcome using a standardized telephone interview assessment tool (GOSE)
items.reasoning: GOSE is a validated standard; the use of structured interviews (Reference 4) limits bias.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Consultees also consented to be contacted for outcome interviews.
items.reasoning: All outcomes were collected via the same interview process at the specified intervals.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounts for several key clinical confounders (age, GCS, CT grade) in the multivariable regression and CCA. However, the very small sample size (n=18) severely limits the ability to adjust for multiple confounders simultaneously without overfitting, and some factors like specific medication effects at the time of EEG were not fully adjusted for.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: clinical variables describing the clinical picture at the time of EEG [age, total GCS score, CT grade... days since injury]
items.reasoning: Key clinical variables were measured, but specific ICU treatments (e.g., specific vasopressors or metabolic state) that could affect EEG were not listed.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: CT grade (1 = No visible intracranial pathology; 6 = non-evacuated mass lesion), days since injury
items.reasoning: The clinical variables used as confounders are standard and well-defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: GCS motor score... CT grade
items.reasoning: These are standard clinical metrics recorded by hospital staff.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: We screened all 139 TBI admissions to the intensive care unit
items.reasoning: Confounders were collected from the same clinical environment (ICU) for all patients.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There was no missing data for the clinical confounders listed in Table 1 for the analyzed group.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use matching or stratification in its design; it relied on post-hoc statistical adjustment.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: stepwise linear regression... using GOSE as the dependent variable and the EEG features and five clinical features above as predictors.
items.reasoning: While adjustment was attempted, the small sample size (n=18) makes the multivariable model unstable and limits the number of confounders that can be reliably included.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (CCA and Stepwise Regression) are appropriate for the exploratory nature of the study. However, stepwise selection is known to be biased in very small samples, and the lack of a pre-registered protocol or a larger validation cohort increases the risk of 'p-hacking' or finding spurious associations.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: We performed a canonical correlation analysis (CCA)... conducted a randomization test with 2000 permutations... stepwise linear regression
items.reasoning: The analytical steps are clearly documented, including the software used.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: stepwise linear regression (entry P = 0.05, removal P = 0.10)
items.reasoning: While based on clinical relevance, stepwise selection in a sample of 18 is statistically risky and can lead to over-optimistic results.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: The GOSE score was normalized using the rank-based inverse Gaussian method
items.reasoning: The authors attempted to correct for non-normality, but the small sample size remains a major limitation for the regression models used.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: All data and analysis scripts are available in the following repository: https://osf.io/8w6qr/
items.reasoning: The provision of raw data and scripts in an OSF repository significantly reduces the risk of selective reporting.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
